text: The barnacle goose is a bird with a strong hold on Irish folklore. It was once counted as a fish. That allowed people to eat it during Lent. The bird was also said to be magical. Older Celtic ideas saw birds as beings made of many elements. This belief may not reach back to ancient myth. It might have grown from later folklore instead. Yet the goose may be older still. Diggers found its bones beneath a Stone Age house. It appears the goose was offered when that home was built. That suggests people saw the bird as a guardian. The goose also flew south to Ireland each year from far away. It vanished and returned in a steady cycle. Those yearly visits made it seem special to the people.

okr.objective: The barnacle goose is a migratory Irish bird once eaten as a fish in Lent, whose foundation-offering bones hint it was a guardian.
key_results: It was counted as a fish, so it could be eaten during the Lenten fast
Its bones were found beneath a Stone Age house, suggesting it was offered as a foundation sacrifice
It is a migratory wildfowl that reached Ireland each year and vanished in a cyclic pattern

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
